Noter - Lektion 7

Johan Ejstrud

2022-04-27

Basic maps (02:24)

  • The Base R function map_data() has that can be used for fast maps. Be aware that the data is low accuracy and out-of-date.
library(tidyverse)

kl <- 
  map_data("world", "greenland") %>% 
  as_tibble()

kl
## # A tibble: 2,240 x 6
##     long   lat group order region    subregion
##    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <chr>     <chr>    
##  1 -46.3  60.8     1     1 Greenland 1        
##  2 -46.4  60.7     1     2 Greenland 1        
##  3 -46.5  60.7     1     3 Greenland 1        
##  4 -46.6  60.7     1     4 Greenland 1        
##  5 -46.7  60.8     1     5 Greenland 1        
##  6 -46.8  60.8     1     6 Greenland 1        
##  7 -46.8  60.8     1     7 Greenland 1        
##  8 -46.4  60.9     1     8 Greenland 1        
##  9 -46.2  60.9     1     9 Greenland 1        
## 10 -46.2  60.9     1    10 Greenland 1        
## # ... with 2,230 more rows
ggplot(kl, aes(long, lat)) +
  geom_point()

Fix coordinate system (05:59)

  • coord_quickmap() sets the same scale for longitude and latitude. (This is a fast approximation of the Mercator projection.)
ggplot(kl, aes(long, lat)) +
  geom_point() + 
  coord_quickmap()

geom_polygon() (03:59)

  • geom_polygon() draws maps as areas. group ensures that the polygons are properly closed.
ggplot(kl, aes(long, lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon() + 
  coord_quickmap()

Zoom (07:00)

  • Use xlim and ylim to zoom.

(The top fjord is Kangerlussuaq; the bottom fjord is Nuup Kangerlua.)

ggplot(kl, aes(long, lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon() + 
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-55, -48), ylim = c(64, 67))

# Store zoom values for later use
nuuk.x <- c(-55, -48)
nuuk.y <- c( 64,  67)
nuuk.close.x <- c(-52.7, -49.6)
nuuk.close.y <- c( 63.8,  65.2)

Simple features (08:05)

  • More complex map data is usually encoded as simple features which requires the package ‘sf’.
library(sf)
  • The package ‘rnaturalearth’ contains simple feature data from https://www.naturalearthdata.com/ .

sf data contains various metadata which makes it complex to look at.

library(rnaturalearth)

kl_sf <- ne_countries(country = "greenland", 
                      returnclass = "sf",
                      scale = "medium")

kl_sf

  • Simple features are plotted with geom_sf(). (We don’t even need to specify aesthetics.)
kl_map <- ggplot(kl_sf) + 
            geom_sf()

nuuk_map <- ggplot(kl_sf) + 
              geom_sf() + 
              coord_sf(xlim = nuuk.x, ylim = nuuk.y)

# Use patchwork package to show multiple plots side-by-side
library(patchwork)
kl_map + nuuk_map

  • Install ‘rnaturalearthhires’ to get access higher resolution data.
# install.packages("devtools")
# devtools::install_github("ropensci/rnaturalearthhires")

kl_sf_high_res <- ne_countries(country = "greenland",
                               returnclass = "sf",
                               scale="large")

ggplot(kl_sf_high_res) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  coord_sf(xlim = nuuk.x, ylim = nuuk.y)

ggplot(kl_sf_high_res) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  coord_sf(xlim = nuuk.close.x, ylim = nuuk.close.y)

Add data on map (13:26)

  • Use the familiar geoms like geom_point() to add data on top of maps.

The package ‘maps’ contains the data set ‘world.cities’ with coordinates of cities around the world.

library(maps)

kl_cities <-
  world.cities %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(country.etc == "Greenland") %>% 
  arrange(-pop)

kl_cities

Points (14:29)

  • The ggplot now uses two data sets, so we need to state which data set each layer uses.
ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = kl_sf) +
  geom_point(data = kl_cities, aes(x = long, y = lat), color = "blue")

Lables (15:43)

  • Add lables with geom_text() or geom_label().
ggplot(kl_sf_high_res) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  coord_sf(xlim = nuuk.close.x, ylim = nuuk.close.y) + 
  geom_point(data = kl_cities, aes(x = long, y = lat), color = "blue") + 
  geom_text(data = kl_cities, aes(x = long, y = lat, label = name))

Projections (16:54)

Map projections are an eternal struggle. Things like geodectic datum, map projection, and parameters have to be considered. Together all of these can be boiled down into a coordinate reference system (CRS).

  • The coordinate reference system (CRS) is stored in the sf data, and can be printed with st_crs().
st_crs(kl_sf)
## Coordinate Reference System:
##   User input: +proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs +ellps=WGS84 +towgs84=0,0,0 
##   wkt:
## BOUNDCRS[
##     SOURCECRS[
##         GEOGCRS["unknown",
##             DATUM["World Geodetic System 1984",
##                 ELLIPSOID["WGS 84",6378137,298.257223563,
##                     LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]],
##                 ID["EPSG",6326]],
##             PRIMEM["Greenwich",0,
##                 ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433],
##                 ID["EPSG",8901]],
##             CS[ellipsoidal,2],
##                 AXIS["longitude",east,
##                     ORDER[1],
##                     ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433,
##                         ID["EPSG",9122]]],
##                 AXIS["latitude",north,
##                     ORDER[2],
##                     ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433,
##                         ID["EPSG",9122]]]]],
##     TARGETCRS[
##         GEOGCRS["WGS 84",
##             DATUM["World Geodetic System 1984",
##                 ELLIPSOID["WGS 84",6378137,298.257223563,
##                     LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]]],
##             PRIMEM["Greenwich",0,
##                 ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
##             CS[ellipsoidal,2],
##                 AXIS["latitude",north,
##                     ORDER[1],
##                     ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
##                 AXIS["longitude",east,
##                     ORDER[2],
##                     ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
##             ID["EPSG",4326]]],
##     ABRIDGEDTRANSFORMATION["Transformation from unknown to WGS84",
##         METHOD["Geocentric translations (geog2D domain)",
##             ID["EPSG",9603]],
##         PARAMETER["X-axis translation",0,
##             ID["EPSG",8605]],
##         PARAMETER["Y-axis translation",0,
##             ID["EPSG",8606]],
##         PARAMETER["Z-axis translation",0,
##             ID["EPSG",8607]]]]
  • coord_sf() can change to any CRS found on https://epsg.io/.
kl_map_crs1 <-
  kl_map +
    coord_sf(crs = st_crs(3189)) # The number for CRS GR96 / UTM zone 29N
    
kl_map_crs2 <-
  kl_map + 
    coord_sf(crs= "+proj=ortho +lat_0=15 +lon_0=-50")

kl_map + kl_map_crs1 + kl_map_crs2

Raster maps (21:01)

Raster maps are based on images instead of vectors.

GeoTiff (21:19)

  • The package ‘stars’ can read GeoTiffs and geom_stars() can plot them as a standard ggplot layer.
library(stars)

tif <- 
  system.file("tif/L7_ETMs.tif", package = "stars") %>% 
  read_stars()

ggplot() + 
  geom_stars(data = tif)

ggmap (22:48)

  • The package ‘ggmap’ can plot data from Stamen and other sources.
  • Use get_stamenmap() to get the image data.
  • Use ggmap() instead of ggplot(). You can add the familiar geoms to ggmap() just like it was ggplot().

www.bboxfinder.com is useful for finding binding boxes.

library(ggmap)

nuuk_bounding_box <- c(left   = min(nuuk.close.x),
                       right  = max(nuuk.close.x),
                       bottom = min(nuuk.close.y),
                       top    = max(nuuk.close.y))

nuuk_stamen <- get_stamenmap(bbox = nuuk_bounding_box, zoom = 8)

ggmap(nuuk_stamen)

Different map types are available.

nuuk_city_bb <- c(left   = -51.76,
                  right  = -51.64,
                  bottom =  64.15,
                  top    =  64.22)

city_zoom <- 12

p1 <- get_stamenmap(bbox = nuuk_city_bb, zoom = city_zoom) %>% 
  ggmap()

p2 <- get_stamenmap(bbox = nuuk_city_bb, zoom = city_zoom, maptype="toner") %>% 
  ggmap()

p3 <- get_stamenmap(bbox = nuuk_city_bb, zoom = city_zoom, maptype="watercolor") %>% 
  ggmap()

p1 + p2 + p3

  • ‘ggmap’ can also be used with google maps, but this requires a google account. (see more: ggmap on GitHub]
